body.heading: One photograph, five memories
paragraphs: Put an old family photograph in the middle of the table and ask everyone what is happening in it. You will get as many photographs as people: one remembers the day, one remembers the argument before it, one is certain the dog was a different dog. The disagreements are not errors; they are the family's history told in surround sound.

Photographs lie politely — everyone smiling, nobody mid-quarrel — and the retelling restores the weather. Children, hearing that the solemn adults in the picture were once caught scrumping apples, receive an important piece of news about grown-ups.

body.heading: Make a habit of the box
paragraphs: A shoebox or album that comes out on a rainy afternoon, a birthday, or when relatives visit, keeps the stories in circulation. Let the oldest person present hold court, and let the youngest ask the questions; both jobs are honours.
Note names and dates on the back of prints, in pencil, while someone still knows them. An unnamed photograph of ancestors becomes, within two generations, a photograph of strangers.

body.heading: New photographs deserve the same treatment
paragraphs: Print a few of this year's pictures — the unposed ones especially — and add them to the box. Future retellings are being stocked now, and the blurry photograph of everyone laughing at something off-camera is the one they will argue about fondly.
Ask the children to choose which pictures go in the box. Their choices — the silly ones, usually — will tell the future what this family found worth keeping.

description: An old photograph retold by the whole family produces five different memories — and that is the point of keeping the box.
